subject: chem
title: Polymerisation
subtitle: Addition and condensation polymers, properties and disposal.
concept: Addition polymers form when alkene monomers undergo addition reactions across their C=C bonds; no small molecule is lost.
Condensation polymers form when difunctional monomers join with loss of a small molecule (H₂O or HCl) at each step.
Polymer properties depend on chain length, branching, cross-linking and the forces between chains; disposal is an environmental concern.

notes.heading: Addition Polymerisation
items: Addition polymers form when many alkene (or substituted alkene) monomers undergo addition across the C=C bond — no atoms are lost. The repeat unit has the same atomic composition as the monomer.

Low-density poly(ethene) (LDPE) is branched — chains cannot pack closely, giving lower density, flexibility, and a lower melting point. High-density poly(ethene) (HDPE, Ziegler–Natta catalyst) has linear chains that pack closely — higher density and melting point.
Addition polymers are chemically inert and non-biodegradable — disposal by landfill or incineration (PVC releases toxic HCl on burning) is problematic.

notes.heading: Condensation Polymerisation
items: Condensation polymers form from difunctional monomers that react together with the loss of a small molecule (usually water, sometimes HCl) at each step.
Polyesters (–COO– linkage): e.g. Terylene/PET from ethane-1,2-diol + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. Polyamides (–CONH– linkage): e.g. nylon-6,6 from hexane-1,6-diamine + hexanedioic acid.
Condensation polymers can be hydrolysed under acidic or basic conditions — unlike addition polymers. This also means they are more biodegradable.

definitions.body: A polymer formed by repeated addition of alkene monomers across C=C double bonds; no small molecule is lost.
A polymer formed by condensation reactions between difunctional monomers, with elimination of a small molecule (H₂O or HCl) at each step.
A small molecule that can undergo polymerisation to form a polymer.

workedExamples.q: Draw a section of nylon-6,6 and identify the amide link.

steps.text: –NH₂ + HOOC– → –NH–CO– + H₂O. One amide bond formed per monomer unit.

mistakes: Drawing the repeat unit of an addition polymer without showing continuation brackets and subscript n.
Confusing the linkage in polyesters (–COO–) with polyamides (–CONH–).
Stating all polymers are non-biodegradable — condensation polymers CAN be hydrolysed; addition polymers cannot.
tips: To write a repeat unit: find the section that repeats. For addition: open the C=C in the monomer and show –[CH₂–CHR]ₙ–.
Nylon-6,6: two types of monomer (each with 6 carbons). Nylon-6: one monomer (caprolactam, ring-opening). Examiners may ask you to distinguish.
PVC produces toxic HCl when incinerated — this is why disposal is controversial.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between addition and condensation polymerisation?
flashcards.a: Addition: alkene monomers add across C=C; no small molecule lost. Condensation: difunctional monomers join with loss of H₂O (or HCl) per bond formed.

flashcards.q: What is the repeat unit of poly(propene)?
What bond links monomers in a polyamide?
flashcards.a: Amide bond: –CO–NH– (formed from –COOH and –NH₂ with loss of H₂O).

flashcards.q: Why can polyesters and polyamides be hydrolysed but poly(ethene) cannot?
flashcards.a: Polyesters and polyamides contain hydrolysable ester/amide bonds; poly(ethene) has only C–C and C–H bonds, which are resistant to hydrolysis.

flashcards.q: Why is incineration of PVC controversial?
flashcards.a: PVC contains chlorine; incineration produces toxic HCl gas and potentially dioxins.

questions.q: Which monomer is used to make poly(chloroethene) (PVC)?
questions.exp: PVC is made by addition polymerisation of chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl).

questions.q: What type of bond is the linkage in a polyester?
questions.exp: Polyesters contain –COO– ester linkages formed from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid with loss of H₂O.

questions.q: Which polymer can be hydrolysed by acid or base?
questions.exp: Nylon-6,6 is a polyamide with hydrolysable amide bonds. Addition polymers (poly(ethene) etc.) cannot be hydrolysed.

questions.q: What small molecule is lost in each step of condensation polymerisation between a diol and a diacid?
questions.exp: Each ester bond formed between –OH and –COOH releases one water molecule.

questions.q: HDPE has higher density and hardness than LDPE because:
opts: It is made at higher temperature
Its chains are more linear, allowing closer packing
questions.exp: HDPE has linear chains (Ziegler–Natta catalyst) → closer packing → higher density and stronger intermolecular forces.

questions.q: What is the repeat unit of poly(chloroethene) (PVC)?
questions.exp: Chloroethene (vinyl chloride, CH₂=CHCl) undergoes addition polymerisation. Each monomer adds across the C=C: the repeat unit is –(CH₂–CHCl)–. PVC is widely used for pipes, cable insulation, and flooring.

questions.q: Why does addition polymerisation give a polymer with 100% atom economy?
opts: All atoms from the monomers are incorporated into the polymer — no by-products
questions.exp: In addition polymerisation, the π bond of each alkene monomer breaks and the monomers join directly with no atoms eliminated. Every atom ends up in the product, so atom economy = 100%. Condensation polymerisation is different — it loses water.

questions.q: Which polymer is formed from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid?
questions.exp: This is a condensation polymerisation forming a polyester: each –OH reacts with –COOH, releasing water and forming an ester linkage (–COO–). The polymer PET (polyethylene terephthalate) is used in bottles, fibres and films.

questions.q: Nylon-6,6 contains amide linkages (–CO–NH–). Which monomers are used?
opts: One diamine and one dicarboxylic acid
One diol and one dicarboxylic acid
questions.exp: Nylon-6,6 is made from hexane-1,6-diamine (H₂N–(CH₂)₆–NH₂) and hexanedioic acid (HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH). Each amine reacts with each acid group, releasing water and forming amide (peptide-like) bonds.

questions.q: How does HDPE differ from LDPE?
opts: HDPE is branched; LDPE is linear
HDPE is linear, allowing closer packing → higher density, melting point and strength
HDPE has a lower molecular mass
HDPE contains chlorine; LDPE does not
questions.exp: HDPE (high-density polyethene) is produced using Ziegler–Natta catalysts, giving linear chains that pack closely → higher density, crystallinity, melting point and tensile strength. LDPE has branched chains (made at high pressure) that prevent close packing.

questions.q: Which type of polymer can be broken down by acid or base hydrolysis?
opts: Neither — all polymers are resistant to hydrolysis
questions.exp: Condensation polymers contain hydrolysable linkages (ester –COO–, amide –CONH–) that can be cleaved by acid or alkali. Addition polymers contain only C–C bonds in the backbone, which are not hydrolysable under normal conditions.

questions.q: What environmental problem is associated with addition polymers?
opts: They release toxic HCl on burning
They are non-biodegradable and persist in the environment
They react with oxygen in air
questions.exp: Addition polymers (poly(ethene), polypropene etc.) have C–C backbones that are not attacked by biological enzymes — they are essentially non-biodegradable and persist for hundreds of years in landfill and oceans.

questions.q: What is 'atom economy'? Calculate it for: A + B → C + D (Mr: A=40, B=60, C=80, D=20)
questions.exp: Atom economy = (Mr desired product / total Mr all products) × 100 = (80/(80+20)) × 100 = 80%. The higher the atom economy, the less waste the process generates.

questions.q: Which monomer would produce a polymer with repeat unit –(CH₂–C(CH₃)₂)–?
questions.exp: 2-Methylpropene (CH₂=C(CH₃)₂) has a C=C with two methyl groups on the same carbon. Addition polymerisation across the double bond gives –(CH₂–C(CH₃)₂)– as the repeat unit (polyisobutylene, used in inner tubes).

questions.q: The tensile strength of Kevlar is due to:
opts: Extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding between amide groups in adjacent chains
Its cross-linked network of covalent bonds
questions.exp: Kevlar is an aromatic polyamide. The amide groups (–CO–NH–) form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds between adjacent polymer chains. Combined with the rigidity of benzene rings, this gives Kevlar exceptional tensile strength (used in bullet-proof vests).

questions.q: Which monomer is used to make poly(propene)?
questions.exp: Poly(propene) forms by addition polymerisation of propene (CH₂=CHCH₃) molecules across the C=C double bond.

questions.q: What small molecule is released during condensation polymerisation of a polyamide?
questions.exp: Polyamides (e.g. nylon) form by condensation between –COOH and –NH₂ groups, releasing H₂O at each step.

questions.q: Nylon-6,6 is formed from two monomers. What are they?
questions.exp: Nylon-6,6 = polyamide from hexane-1,6-diamine (6C diamine) + hexanedioic acid (6C diacid). Each unit loses H₂O to form –CONH– linkage.

questions.q: Why is poly(chloroethene) PVC problematic when incinerated?
questions.exp: PVC contains C–Cl bonds. Burning releases HCl gas, which is toxic and corrosive.

questions.q: HDPE (high-density polyethene) has a higher melting point than LDPE because:
opts: HDPE chains are more linear and pack more closely — stronger intermolecular forces
questions.exp: LDPE has branched chains (from free-radical initiation) that can't pack tightly. HDPE (Ziegler–Natta catalyst) is linear → closer packing → stronger id–id forces → higher mp.

questions.q: Terylene (PET) is a polyester made from ethane-1,2-diol and:
questions.exp: PET/Terylene: ethane-1,2-diol + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid → polyester with –COO– linkages, releasing H₂O.

questions.q: Addition polymers are generally non-biodegradable because:
opts: They have no hydrolysable backbone linkages
questions.exp: Addition polymers have a C–C backbone with no ester or amide bonds — enzymes and water cannot hydrolyse them, making them persistent in the environment.

questions.q: The repeat unit of poly(tetrafluoroethene) PTFE is:
questions.exp: PTFE (Teflon) forms from tetrafluoroethene (CF₂=CF₂) by addition polymerisation. The repeat unit is –(CF₂–CF₂)–.

questions.q: Condensation polymers, unlike addition polymers, can be hydrolysed because:
questions.exp: Ester (–COO–) and amide (–CONH–) linkages in condensation polymers can be cleaved by water under acid or base conditions — reverse of condensation.

questions.q: The atom economy of addition polymerisation is:
questions.exp: Addition polymerisation has 100% atom economy — only one product is formed (the polymer) and no atoms are wasted.

recall: Distinguish between addition and condensation polymerisation.
